zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check only, after independent scan reading: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; Hideyuki Ohshima, with Taichi Aida; source licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). Transcription choices and English review notes here are this reviewer's scan-based work, not a reproduction of the headword dataset.

lines.note: Gon completes jo-gon from f292, not a new headword. The sentence says that giving advice during the games is a cause of quarrels; the printed motoigia is retained rather than simplified to a modern moto ja.

runs.text: go do Go, & enxadrez o falar, ou terçar por

lines.note: Completes jogo from the preceding row. The Portuguese explains talking or taking a side during go and chess; Go is a Japanese game-name embedded in this italic explanation.

runs.text: hũa parte he ocaſião de brigas.

lines.note: Completes the warning that siding with one player gives occasion for quarrels. The opening three rows are continuations and are indented like the surrounding continuation text.
Joogowai means obstinate; the dictionary prefers the separated expression joo no kowai. The initial is I, not OCR long s; Meliùs is italic editorial apparatus.
Completes the obstinacy gloss with stubborn. It is not a separate entry.
Joogowana is an adjectival alternative with the same meaning. Idem refers to the immediately preceding stubbornness definition.
Joogowani is the corresponding adverb, stubbornly. Adu. is the italic grammatical label; the initial I lost by OCR is present.
Joogu is seeking what is higher, ue wo motomuru, rendered by the Portuguese as salvation. The object marker uo should not be interpreted as possessive no.
The example enjoins not neglecting the practice of seeking enlightenment. Vocotarazare is the printed negative imperative; it is not modernized.

runs.text: Não vos deſcuideis no negocio da ſaluação.

lines.note: Translates the injunction as not becoming negligent in the business of salvation. S. is an upright written-register label.
Joogai is outside the fortress, shiro no hoka. The initial I omitted by OCR is visible.
Joogan is the first book or upper volume, ue no maki. The Portuguese explanation continues with its place in a larger work.

runs.text: parte dalgum corpo, & volume de liuro.

lines.note: Completes the description as part of a collected body or volume of a book. It belongs to joogan.
Jooge is above and below, explicitly ue and shita. The headword's initial I corrects the OCR lowercase i.
Adds the social sense, the high and the low. The example begins with jooge and is completed on the next line.
Completes jooge banmin, all people, high and low. Enlargement supports n in banmin rather than OCR u; Itẽ is an abbreviation of Item followed by a comma, not a word broken by a terminal hyphen.
Adds the verbal interpretation of jooge: going up and coming down. The paired Japanese forms are nobori and kudaru; Vt introduces a travel example.
The example concerns repeatedly going up to and returning from the capital. Camiye is the directional phrase, while the Portuguese continuation makes the frequency explicit.
Completes the translation as frequent travel to and from Miyako. Miyaco is italic in the Portuguese sentence and is not normalized to the Miaco spelling used elsewhere.
Joogen, explained by ue moto, refers to the fifteenth day of the first lunar month. The printed Portuguese date expression and abbreviated lũa are retained without expanding them.
Joogyoo is pure conduct or good works, explained by isagiyoku okonoo. The scan's long-o marks are preserved; the Portuguese qualifies the works further below.
Completes the definition as pure works. Bup. is the upright Buddhist-register label, including its final punctuation.
Jooi is an order of the Kuboo. Cubǒ is upright within the Portuguese explanation; meſ- starts the additional sense, the ruler himself.
Completes meſmo Cubǒ, the Kuboo himself, then broadens the meaning to an order of another great lord. The second title is also upright.
Completes senhor grande and supplies Tono as another lordly designation. Tono is a Japanese title embedded in the Portuguese explanation, regardless of its printed type.
This separate jooi denotes a good or excellent physician. Fiſico has its historical medical sense, not the modern sense of a physicist.
Jooji, joozuru, joojita means mounting or boarding, explicitly noru. The principal-part endings are retained rather than replaced with modernized forms.

runs.text: carſe. ¶ Item, Estar enleuado, ou abſor-

lines.note: Completes embarcarſe and adds being engrossed or absorbed. The second sense is figurative and continues below.
Completes abſorto em alguma cousa. Kangen kyoo ni begins an example about absorption in the delight of music.

runs.text: Eſtar embebido no gosto da muſica.

lines.note: Joozuru completes the music example. The Portuguese says to be engrossed in the enjoyment of music; the circumflex is retained.

runs.text: Peßoas que ſeruem na Tera, ou aos Bõ-

lines.note: Jooji denotes people serving at a temple or attending the Bonzos. The scan reads ſeruem na Tera, not ſeruemu na Pera. On the second pass, the lowercase letters of Tera clearly match the surrounding italic type; the word is retained in that italic span rather than normalized to roman. The capital T alone is less diagnostic, so its typeface remains a minor caveat for the whole-word toggle.

runs.text: zos. ¶ Item, Homem que tem por offi-

lines.note: Completes Bõzos and adds a person whose occupation is specified below. The terminal offi- visibly divides officio.
Completes the preceding definition of Iôji: a person whose occupation is to ring the bell; the initial cio belongs to the divided Portuguese offi-cio.
Vye vye, 'above above', explains the superlative jōjō; the Portuguese says supreme or excellent. Retain the tilde in excelẽte and distinguish the two caroned vowels in the headword.

runs.text: Hum dos cinco liuros, que enſinão a go-

lines.note: The book title is identified as one of five books teaching government. The scan supports initial I, not long ſ, and a space between a and the divided go-; the final vowel of the headword is unmarked.
Completes go-uernar, 'to govern', from the preceding physical line; this is not a separate entry.
Taſuqe naſu supplies the sense of helping or bringing rescue; the Portuguese says save and deliver from dangers. The first o of Iojǒ is unmarked, unlike its final ǒ.

runs.text: rigos, ou ſocorrer em neceßidades, &c. Vt,

lines.note: Completes pe-rigos, then adds assistance in needs or difficulties. Retain the printed ß in neceßidades and the example introducer Vt.
The honorific Japanese request asks for assistance, matching 'I ask that you ...'. A visible word space separates Gojojǒuo from tanomi; zonzuru remains a separate word.
Completes the Portuguese request: help me and do me a kindness. Retain the unaccented final merce rather than modernizing its spelling.
Jōju is explained as perfecting or completing; Xoguã begins the Japanese example about a wish. The entire Japanese word is roman, including its final nasalized ã.
Completes the Japanese example as bringing the wish to accomplishment. The Portuguese gives fulfilment, with the printed ef- continuing onto the next line.
Completes ef-feituarſe and identifies the thing fulfilled as someone's wish. Preserve the historical spelling and long ſ in deſejo rather than regularizing the divided verb.
Cami tôca identifies the first ten days, confirmed by the Portuguese definition. The Japanese is Cami, not the OCR Camri; the mark on tôca is a circumflex.
Completes 'the first ten days of the month'; the single word is the continuation of the Iǒjun entry.

runs.text: Arroz que ſe mete na fortaleza pera

lines.note: The headword is Iǒmai, rice put into a fortress. The scan has initial I and no additional i between ǒ and m; this corrects the misleading OCR form.
Completes the definition of fortress rice as provisions and victuals. Retain pera from the preceding line and the historical vitualha here.
Qiyoqu aqiracana combines purity and brightness, matching the Portuguese 'pure and ...'. Both marked vowels in the headword are caroned.
Completes 'pure and clear'. The final upright S. is outside the italic Portuguese; the row is visibly indented like other continuations.
The second homographic entry means something always clear or bright, as Tçuneni aqiraca nari explains. Preserve the abbreviation q̃ and the physical division ſem-pre.
Completes the adverb ſem-pre and the explanation 'is always clear'; està bears the printed grave accent.
Yaqi foroboſu, destruction by burning, is glossed as a burning of houses. The first marked o is circumflexed and the second caroned; these differing marks are visible in the type.
The Japanese injunction calls for vigilance against a conflagration. Preserve the marks in Iômǒno and yôjin; the Portuguese ha- continues as haja on the next row.
Completes the warning to guard against burning or fire. The initial ja is the second portion of the previous line's ha-ja.
Xirono vchi, inside the castle, directly agrees with the Portuguese definition 'within the fortress'.
Tçuneni vomô explains continual thought; the Portuguese gives always thinking or ... . Keep the circumflex in vomô.
Completes the definition as continuous thoughts. The terminal S. is printed upright and is separated from the italic explanation.
Vye atçui indicates heat above; the Portuguese describes blood rising to the head. Restore the visible initial I in Iǒnet and keep all of Vye in roman rather than italicizing only its initial.
The adverb is defined as 'much in quantity'. Preserve cantidade, the historical Portuguese spelling, rather than silently replacing it with quantidade.
The Japanese phrase describes stubbornness, matching 'hard and obstinate'; this is the alternative form cited earlier under Iǒgouai.
The corresponding nominal expression denotes obstinacy. Keep the long ſ in couaſa and the unaccented Portuguese Pertinacia.
Iſaguiyoqu qiyoxi describes thorough purity, confirmed by the Portuguese 'very clean'. The headword's vowel mark is visibly a caron, not the draft's circumflex.
Completes lim-pa and adds 'pure'; this continuation belongs to the first Iǒqet entry rather than the following homograph.
This homographic Iǒqet is defined as a principal place or city, not the purity sense of the preceding entry; the caroned headword is retained.
Qiga agaru describes a rising of qi; the Portuguese explains blood and humours rising to the head. Preserve the physical division hu-mores.
Completes the Portuguese explanation and supplies past and present Japanese forms. The example begins with capital I, not lowercase l; the later l, is the printed alternative marker.

runs.text: Boa cõpreiſão, ou vigor de homẽ forte,

lines.note: The Portuguese defines a strong constitution or the vigour of a strong person, clarified by the following perseverance example. Retain the unusual visible cõpreiſão and the nasal abbreviation homẽ rather than substituting a modern form.
Completes the description of a strong, persevering person, then begins an example of doing something with sustained vigour. The paragraph sign is genuine print, not a letter.

runs.text: Fazer algũa couſa com vigor, & for-

lines.note: Finishes the Japanese verb and begins its Portuguese rendering, doing something with vigour and strength. Retain the tilde on algũa and the divided for-ça.
Completes 'strength, without tiring or ceasing'; the two long ſ characters in ceſſar are retained.
Miacoye noboru, going up to the capital, agrees with 'go to Miaco'. Both o vowels in the headword carry carons; Miacoye has no extra nasal letter.
The entry means something excellent. The terminal S. is roman, outside the italic Portuguese definition.
Xiro supplies the synonym 'castle', glossed as fortress. The following example begins with a physically divided Iǒqua-cu; preserve the printed hyphen.
Completes Iǒquacu with the object marker uo and the verb camayuru; the Portuguese explains enclosing or fortifying the fortress.
Completes the object of 'enclose or fortify'; this is an indented continuation, not a new fortress headword.
Teiuǒ gives the sovereign sense, rendered as king. The initial is visibly I, not the draft's t; retain the printed vowel marks even though the synonym and definition guide the lexical reading.
Tçuneni tanoximu explains continual enjoyment, matching the Portuguese continuous delights. Preserve the split gos-tos.
Completes delights and pleasures, then begins the Buddhist phrase about lasting bliss and purity/selfhood. The transcription retains the actual gajǒno rather than expanding its doctrinal terms.
Completes the Japanese statement about such a place; the Portuguese identifies the place of blessedness. Benauenturança is one word: the draft's internal space is not a word boundary in the scan.
Completes the rendering of the blissful place as one with perpetual contentment; retain the grave accent in hà.
Xirono vchi again means inside the castle, agreeing exactly with 'within the fortress'. The smudging at the headword does not justify changing its visible Iǒri.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Cidade principal, & grande, à ſe-

lines.note: Adds the sense of a principal, large city, with a comparison continued on the next row. Preserve the paragraph sign and the divided ſe-melhança.

runs.text: melhança da qual ſe fazem as fortalezas.

lines.note: Completes the statement that fortresses are made in the likeness of such a city. The scan separates qual from ſe; the draft's qualſe join is removed.

runs.text: Certa laya de calçado como alparcas.

lines.note: A separate homograph denotes footwear resembling alparcas, i.e. straw or light sandals. Preserve the headword's caron and the historical Portuguese laya.

runs.text: Meliùs, Xǒriacu. O cortar, ou ſin-

lines.note: The preferred form Xǒriacu refers to initial shortening or elision, explained in the following example. Its vowel has a caron, not a grave; the word is set in italic with the surrounding explanation, rather than being normalized to roman.

runs.text: copar algũa palaura no principio. Vt,

lines.note: Completes ſin-copar and specifies dropping the beginning of a word. Sori is the standalone Japanese example and is printed roman.

runs.text: Em lugar de Cami ſori. ¶ Item, No tan-

lines.note: Em, not Eim, introduces the full form Cami ſori for which Sori substitutes. Cami ſori is embedded in the Portuguese sentence and printed italic; the next sense concerns abbreviated instrumental playing.

runs.text: ger abreuiar, ou fazer que não ſoẽ algũas

lines.note: Completes tan-ger and explains omitting the sounding of certain strokes. Keep the tilde in ſoẽ and in algũas rather than expanding either form.

runs.text: pancadas no principio, & aßi em outras cou-

lines.note: Specifies that the omitted strokes are at the beginning and extends the comparison to other things. Preserve the ß in aßi and the divided cou-ſas.

Completes cou-ſas and cross-refers to Chûriacu and Cariacu, shortening in the middle or latter part. The scan shows an upward circumflex on û in Chûriacu, not the draft's grave accent; both cross-reference headwords are roman.
Naritatçu supplies becoming established or accomplished, glossed as perfecting. The final upright S has no securely visible period, so none is supplied.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de bordanſinho curto que

lines.note: This Iorǒ is a short support-stick, not the differently accented catchword below. The first o is unmarked, the last has a caron; retain the printed bordanſinho rather than modernizing the diminutive.

runs.text: ſerue no Zaxiqui aos velhos, & outras peſſoas

lines.note: The support is used by older and other people in the Zaxiqui, the sitting room. Zaxiqui has a capital Z and is printed italic within the Portuguese; peſſoas contains two long ſ letters, not the OCR t.

runs.text: ſobre que eſtribão o queixo de baixo.

lines.note: Completes the explanation: the lower chin rests on the support. The first word is ſobre, not ſebre; preserve the separate de baixo.

zones.label: Gathering signature
zones.note: The large O followed by a smaller lowercase o is separate from the catchword to its right.
